history: The third generation Honda Civic, introduced for 1983, marked a pivotal moment in the model's history. This was the generation where the Civic grew up — adopting a more aerodynamic, modern design language that looked genuinely contemporary rather than merely efficient. The boxy styling of the first two generations gave way to a sleeker, more angular shape that reflected the design trends of the early 1980s.

Under the hood, Honda introduced a new family of engines with improved power and refinement. The headline addition was the 1.5-liter dual-carburetor engine producing 76 horsepower — a significant jump over previous offerings that gave the Civic a genuine performance character for the first time. Combined with the 5-speed manual transmission, the third-gen Civic could hold its own against much of the competition.

The most significant addition to the third-generation lineup was the introduction of the Civic Si in 1984 — a high-performance variant with a tuned 1.5-liter engine, sport suspension, and a more aggressive appearance. The Si established the performance sub-brand that would eventually lead to the Type R, making this generation historically crucial to the Civic's enthusiast legacy.

Honda also introduced the CRX alongside the third-gen Civic, sharing its platform and engines. The CRX's lightweight two-seat formula and exceptional fuel economy made it an instant hit and one of the most beloved Hondas ever built. Together, the third-gen Civic and CRX cemented Honda's reputation for building cars that were simultaneously efficient, reliable, and genuinely fun to drive.
did_you_know: The third-generation Civic was the first generation to offer the Civic Si performance variant, which debuted in Japan in 1984 before arriving in North America in 1986. The Si name — standing for "Sport Injection" — referred to its fuel-injected engine, a relative rarity on economy cars at the time and a genuine technical achievement for Honda.

trims.name: Civic Base
trims.description: The entry-level third-gen with the 1.3L engine, 5-speed manual, and the new more aerodynamic body style that looked far more modern than its predecessors.

trims.name: Civic DX
trims.description: The mid-range DX trim adding a more complete feature set including a rear wiper, upgraded audio, and improved interior materials. The most popular choice for everyday buyers.

trims.name: Civic GL
trims.description: The premium standard trim with the 1.5L dual-carburetor engine, additional comfort features, and the most refined interior available outside of the Si.

trims.name: Civic Si
trims.description: The landmark performance variant arriving in North America for 1986. Fuel-injected 1.5L engine producing 91 hp, sport suspension, unique body kit, and the Si badging that would become synonymous with Honda performance.

variants.name: Civic Si
variants.description: The introduction of the Si to North America for 1986 was a watershed moment for Honda enthusiasts. With 91 horsepower from a fuel-injected 1.5L engine and a sport-tuned chassis, it was quick, nimble, and affordable — the first truly driver-focused Civic available in the US market.

variants.name: Honda CRX
variants.description: Sharing the third-gen Civic's platform and engines, the CRX was a two-seat sports car disguised as an economy car. The CRX Si in particular — with 91 hp and a featherweight 1,900-pound curb weight — became one of the most beloved Hondas ever sold and a formative influence on an entire generation of enthusiasts.

variants.name: Civic Wagon
variants.description: The practical wagon variant continued into the third generation, now offered with 4-wheel drive on some markets — an unusual feature for a compact wagon in 1983 and a genuine differentiator in the segment.
